structure.title: Preface
structure.summary:
- This is the Sustainability Statement within Belfius Bank’s Annual Report 2024 (Management Report section).
- The contents are structured into six parts: I) General information, II) Environmental information, III) Social information, IV) Governance information, V) Auditor’s limited assurance report, and VI) Appendix.
- Purpose: to present Belfius Group’s strategy, business model, governance, risks and opportunities, performance, and future outlook on sustainable development, and to link sustainability matters to the Group’s activities, governance, and decisions in 2024.
- Reporting framework and scope: prepared on a consolidated basis in line with the CSRD (as transposed into Belgian law on 28 November 2024), ESRS (EFRAG), and the EU Taxonomy Regulation (2020/852) with the related Disclosure Delegated Act (2021/2178); consolidation scope aligns with Belfius’ consolidated financial statements.
- Belfius Insurance does not publish a separate consolidated CSRD report because it is included in Belfius Bank’s consolidated sustainability statement.
- Double materiality: a comprehensive assessment started in 2023 and continued in 2024, covering impacts, risks, and opportunities across upstream and downstream value chains; further detail is in section 1.6. No IP, know-how, or innovation results were omitted when defining materiality.
- ESG coverage: material impacts, risks, and opportunities are addressed for environmental, social, and governance topics across direct operations and indirect business relationships.
- Time horizons for assessing impacts, risks, and opportunities: short term (1 year), medium term (1–5 years), and long term (>5 years), with any deviations disclosed in relevant sections.
- Estimates and proxies: key areas include GHG emissions (section 2.2) and climate risk (section 2.3). Data sources include client-provided data, external vendors, sector averages where needed, and combined sources (e.g., for financed emissions). Methods and data are under continuous improvement, with assumptions and judgments governed and disclosed.
- Certain datapoints are included by reference (details not shown in the excerpt).

structure.title: General information
structure.heading: I. General information
structure.start_phrase:
The 2024 Belfius Sustainability Statement is designed to present the Belfius Group (“Belfius”) strategy, business 
model, governance, risks and opportunities, performance and future outlook with regard to sustainable 
development.
structure.summary:
- Purpose and scope of the 2024 Belfius Sustainability Statement
  - Integrated part of the annual report, explaining strategy, business model, governance, risks/opportunities, performance and outlook on sustainable development.
  - Prepared in line with CSRD (transposed into Belgian law), ESRS, and EU Taxonomy; same consolidation scope as financial statements; Belfius Insurance consolidated and exempt from separate CSRD.
  - Full application of double materiality across upstream and downstream value chains; no omission of IP/know‑how.

- Basis for preparation, assumptions and transitional relief
  - Time horizons defined: short (1 year), medium (1–5 years), long (>5 years).
  - Use of estimates and proxies, notably for GHG emissions (financed and operational) and climate risk; multiple data sources, sector averages and continuous improvement.
  - Information included by reference where appropriate; transitional reliefs applied for entity-specific disclosures, value-chain data limitations, comparative information, and phased-in ESRS requirements (E1-9; S1-7; S1-12).
  - Reporting process, internal controls and assurance: Finance coordinates; ESG Central sets methodologies; second-line Risk review; internal audit performed on carbon accounting and climate risk; key reporting risks identified with mitigations (data quality, automation, consistency, greenwashing, regulatory evolution).

- Business model and strategy
  - Belgian state-owned integrated bank-insurer with core operations in Belgium; specific entities in Luxembourg and Ireland.
  - Three core client segments: Individuals (incl. Private/Wealth), Public & Social sector (PSB), and Entrepreneurs & Enterprises (E&E).
  - Strategy: digital-leading, universal bank-insurer focused on customer centricity, societal value, disciplined risk/financial management; sustainability embedded via “Walk the talk” and “Customers in the driver’s seat.”
  - Progress on six Inspire 2025 commitments (own footprint reduction exceeded; renewable electricity share; charity support; women in management; meaningful investment production; financing future-proof infrastructure).
  - Ongoing strategic refresh toward 2030.

- Value chain and stakeholder engagement
  - Deeply embedded in Belgian economy; reinvests deposits into local projects.
  - Systematic, multi-channel engagement with customers, regulators, employees, independent networks, shareholder, investors/ratings agencies, strategic partners, suppliers, reinsurers, asset management counterparties, civil society/NGOs, sector federations, and supranational/local sustainability initiatives.
  - Stakeholder input informs due diligence and materiality; adjustments made to distribution/accessibility in 2024.

- Governance integration of sustainability
  - Board of Directors oversees strategy, policies, risk appetite (increasing ESG integration); Risk Committee and Audit Committee support and monitor.
  - Management Board implements strategy; fit & proper focus includes ESG; competence matrix includes ESG; targeted ESG upskilling (e.g., Board seminar).
  - Joint Management Committee manages group ESG strategy/regulation; specialist ESG teams and committees (ESG Central, ESG Risk Competence Centre, ESG methodology desk, ESG Models Steering Committee).
  - Regular Board/Management discussions on ESG topics (own footprint targets, security and data protection, customer transparency, innovation/digitalization, financial inclusion, resilience, meaningful financing/investing/insurance, policy reviews).
  - Board composition and diversity statistics; variable remuneration includes ESG KPIs (social, environmental, governance), with 9.8% ESG weighting in 2024 and function-specific ESG objectives.

- Due diligence framework
  - Mapping of ESRS due-diligence core elements to report sections: embedding in governance/strategy, stakeholder engagement, impact identification/assessment, action, and effectiveness tracking.

- Double Materiality Assessment (DMA)
  - 2024 DMA aligned with ESRS: scope covers own operations and full value chain (financing, investment, insurance, suppliers).
  - Inputs from ESRS topics, peer/desk research (ECB/EIOPA guidance, SASB, UNEP FI, NGFS), prior assessments, media; quantitative enrichment using UNEP FI Impact Analysis and ENCORE proxies; alignment with internal risk processes.
  - Risks assessed gross of mitigations; opportunities tied to existing strategy; validated by internal stakeholders and governance bodies.

- Material sustainability matters identified
  - Environmental: own climate footprint; meaningful financing, investing and insurance (impact and financial materiality; downstream focus).
  - Social: own workforce; customer transparency; financial inclusion; information security/data protection; innovation & digitalization; community involvement.
  - Governance: business conduct; resilience; sustainable procurement.
  - Climate approach: Climate & Environmental Policy (CEP) for own ops; Transition Acceleration Policy (TAP) phases out coal by 2030, constrains oil/gas and electricity generation; climate risks and opportunities integrated in lending, investment and insurance; biodiversity and deforestation considerations in sector policies.

- Environmental information highlights
  - Strong focus on reducing own footprint; CEP sets objectives for energy efficiency, renewable energy, water, biodiversity, waste and pollution in own operations; applies group-wide; linked to management incentives; approved by JMC and published.
  - Climate risk/opportunity disclosure aligned with TCFD; financed emissions measured per PCAF with improving data quality; role as transition financier emphasized.
  - Integration of climate-related and environmental risks into risk management per ECB guidance.
  - Insurance taxonomy: assessment of non-life revenues contributing to climate adaptation; NatCat protection offerings to support resilience.
  - No specific targets on pollution, water/marine, circular economy, and biodiversity given business nature, while focusing on carbon reduction, renewables financing, and energy efficiency.
  - Introduction to carbon accounting methodology (scope and methods to follow).

structure.title: Environmental information
structure.heading: II. Environmental information
structure.start_phrase: Belfius puts a strong focus on reducing its own climate footprint .
structure.summary:
- Overview of Belfius’ Climate & Environmental Policy (CEP), focused on reducing its own climate footprint and supporting a low‑carbon, resilient and environmentally sustainable society.
- Scope of CEP: applies to all subsidiaries under Belfius’ operational control; covers climate change mitigation and adaptation, building energy efficiency, renewable energy for data centers, water use and preservation, biodiversity, waste reduction, and pollution prevention in own operations.
- Governance and accountability: every division and employee must apply the policy; managers’ variable pay linked to annually updated ESG objectives; policy implemented by the Head of People Brand Communication and ESG and approved by the JMC; public availability and linkage to corporate governance.
- Climate risk management and transparency: alignment with TCFD for measuring and disclosing climate‑related risks and opportunities.
- Financed emissions measurement: accounting for GHG emissions from loans and investments using PCAF, with commitment to improve data quality and completeness.
- Role as financial intermediary: financing and engaging clients to enable their transition; guided by a Transition Action Plan (TAP).
- Sector policies and exclusions: no financing of coal extraction; full phase‑out of financial support to thermal coal across the value chain by 2030; limitations on oil and gas activities; decreasing thresholds for electricity generation.
- Integration of climate and environmental risks into Belfius’ risk framework in line with the ECB’s guidance, reflecting impacts on counterparties and collateral values.
- Insurance contributions to adaptation: measurement of non‑life revenues aligned with EU Taxonomy for climate adaptation; offering Natural Catastrophe coverage to support client and societal resilience.
- Note on other environmental topics: no specific targets for pollution, water/marine resources, circular economy, or biodiversity given business nature, but continued focus on carbon reduction, renewable energy financing, energy efficiency, and responsible practices.
- Forthcoming detail: introduction to Section 2.1 on carbon accounting methodology and its scope.

nodes.title: Environmental Information - Introduction
nodes.heading: 2. Environmental Information

nodes.summary: This introductory section outlines Belfius’ Climate and Environmental Policy (CEP), applicable to all subsidiaries under operational control, targeting climate mitigation/adaptation in operations and with clients, building energy efficiency, renewable energy for data centres, and operational water, biodiversity, waste and pollution aspects. Governance includes implementation by the Head of People Brand Communication and ESG, approval by the JMC, and ESG-linked variable pay for managers; all divisions and employees must apply the CEP, which is published on Belfius’ website. Belfius measures and discloses climate-related risks and opportunities per TCFD, accounts for financed emissions via PCAF (noting data limitations and ongoing improvement), and engages clients to finance their transition under its TAP. Exclusion and transition policies include no coal extraction financing and a phase-out of thermal coal along the value chain by 2030, limits on oil and gas, and decreasing thresholds for electricity generation. Climate and environmental risks are being integrated into risk management per the ECB Guide; Belfius Insurance measures non-life revenues contributing to climate adaptation under the EU Taxonomy and offers Natural Catastrophe coverage. Belfius notes no specific targets/policies for pollution, water/marine resources, circular economy and biodiversity, while focusing on carbon footprint reduction, renewable financing and energy efficiency. The section leads into 2.1 on carbon accounting methodology.

nodes.title: Scope and methodology of Belfius carbon calculation
nodes.heading: 2.1.1. Scope and methodology of Belfius carbon calculation
nodes.start_phrase: Belfius’ carbon footprint is calculated for the Belfius Group according to the operational control consolidation approach, i.e. entities over which Belfius has the full authority to introduce and implement operating policies.
nodes.summary:
- Focus and governance: Belfius’ Climate & Environmental Policy (CEP) targets mitigation, adaptation, energy efficiency, renewable energy, water use, biodiversity, waste reduction and pollution prevention across all group entities under operational control. Implementation is led by the Head of People Brand Communication & ESG, approved by the JMC, and embedded in governance and incentives (manager variable pay linked to ESG objectives).

- Transparency and frameworks: Belfius measures and discloses climate-related risks and opportunities in line with TCFD, and integrates climate and environmental risks into its risk framework per the ECB Guide.

- Financing the transition: The bank’s largest environmental impact stems from financing, leasing, insurance and asset management. It engages clients to reduce emissions and follows a Transition Action Plan (TAP) that:
  - Excludes financing coal extraction and phases out thermal coal across the value chain by 2030.
  - Limits oil and gas activities to balance a socially inclusive transition with international climate targets.
  - Sets decreasing thresholds for electricity generation activities.
  Belfius Insurance assesses adaptation-aligned revenues under the EU Taxonomy and provides Natural Catastrophe coverage to support climate resilience.

- Scope of environmental topics: While not setting specific targets for pollution, water/marine resources, circular economy, or biodiversity, Belfius prioritizes reducing its carbon footprint, financing renewables, improving energy efficiency, and promoting responsible practices.

- Carbon accounting boundaries and standards: Group carbon accounting follows the operational control approach and aligns with the GHG Protocol and PCAF. All seven UNFCCC gases are reported in CO2e using reputable emission factors (ADEME, DEFRA, Ecoinvent, IEA). Unconsolidated investees fall under Scope 3 Category 15.

- Emission scopes and categories:
  - Scope 1: Direct emissions from building fuels, company cars, and refrigerants.
  - Scope 2: Indirect emissions from purchased electricity/heat.
  - Scope 3 (own operations): Upstream (Categories 1–8) including purchased goods/services, capital goods, fuel and energy-related activities, transport, waste, business travel, commuting/telework, and leased assets; Downstream (Categories 11–14) including use of digital channels, end-of-life of sold products (e.g., cards), downstream leased assets (e.g., leased cars, insurance-owned buildings), and franchises. Some categories are not material.
  - Scope 3 (financed emissions, Category 15): Mortgages, commercial real estate, business & corporate loans, equities & bonds, project finance (renewables), motor vehicle loans, financial leases, and sovereign bonds. Construction/renovation loans are currently excluded due to methodology gaps; Belfius plans to add embodied emissions for real estate when feasible. Financial leases are aligned using relevant PCAF asset methodologies.

- Methodological notes: No carbon removals, credits, transfers, or avoided emissions are included. Biofuels are accounted for per EU Renewable Energy Directive with separate biogenic accounting.

- Data quality and improvement: Own-operations emissions rely mainly on primary data from suppliers and internal stakeholders. Financed emissions use client-reported data, ESG data providers, and PCAF emission factors, with data quality tracked via PCAF scores (1 = highest quality, 5 = broad estimates). Belfius applies the precautionary principle, documents assumptions, and runs a data improvement plan to expand reported data and reduce estimates. CSRD is expected to enhance data availability.

- Reporting and targets: Belfius annually measures and discloses GHG emissions per GHG Protocol and PCAF. Decarbonization targets start with own operations where the bank has strongest control and leverage.

nodes.title: Data quality
nodes.heading: 2.1.2. Data quality
nodes.start_phrase: Belfius encounters difficulties in obtaining complete, accurate and consistent data when assessing its carbon footprint.
nodes.summary:
- Context: Extract from Belfius Bank’s 2024 Annual Report (Management Report – Sustainability Statement), focusing on Category 15 (Investment/financed emissions), data quality, and GHG emissions approach.
- Financed emissions scope: Lists asset classes and scopes covered, including mortgages (Scopes 1–2), commercial real estate (Scopes 1–2), business & corporate loans (Scopes 1–3), equities & bonds (Scopes 1–3), project finance (Scopes 1–2), motor vehicle loans (Scopes 1–2), financial lease (Scopes 1–2), and sovereign bonds (Scopes 1–2).
- Data quality challenges: Notes difficulties in obtaining complete, accurate, and consistent data; fluctuations may reflect methodology refinements and improved data rather than real emission changes.
- Data quality metric: “Data quality percentage” shows the share of emissions calculated with actual reported data versus totals (referenced in an “Operational Emissions – by scope and category” table).
- Own operations data: For all scopes/categories except Category 15, 2024 calculations rely on primary activity data collected from suppliers and internal stakeholders rather than estimates.
- Financed emissions data sources and methods: Uses client-reported or ESG provider GHG data; applies PCAF emission factors to convert activity data to CO2e.
- PCAF data quality scoring: Score 1 = highest quality (actual company/asset emissions); Score 5 = broad estimates based on sector averages. Scores guide prioritization of estimation methods and continuous improvement (referenced in “Financed emissions by asset class” table in section 2.2.1).
- Methodological principles: Prioritizes most recent, highest-quality data; aligns with GHG Protocol and PCAF; follows UN precautionary principle; documents all assumptions and estimates for future updates.
- Continuous improvement: Active data improvement plan to increase reported data and reduce generalized estimates; expects CSRD to enhance data accessibility for financing and investment activities.
- GHG emissions management: Belfius annually measures and discloses GHG emissions across operations under GHG Protocol and PCAF; climate targets start with emissions under full operational control, focusing on areas with greatest leverage to drive decarbonization.

nodes.title: GHG Emissions
nodes.heading: 2.2. GHG Emissions
nodes.start_phrase: Belfius yearly measures and discloses its GHG emissions across all its operations according to the GHG Protocol and PCAF methodologies.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on financed emissions (Scope 3, Category 15) across key asset classes: mortgages, commercial real estate, business & corporate loans, equities & bonds, project finance, motor vehicle loans, financial lease, and sovereign bonds.
- Data quality framework and challenges: variability driven by methodology refinements and data completeness; data quality percentage reflects share of emissions based on actual reported data. Own operational emissions use primary activity data. Financed emissions rely on client-reported/ESG-provider data and PCAF emission factors, with PCAF data quality scores (1=highest, 5=lowest) used to track and improve calculation quality.
- Commitment to best-available data and standards: alignment with GHG Protocol and PCAF; application of the UN precautionary principle; thorough documentation of assumptions; ongoing data improvement plan aiming to increase reported data, decrease estimates; CSRD expected to enhance data access.
- Emissions performance (2022–2024): financed emissions rose 11% in 2024 to 26.78 MtCO2e; operational emissions fell 7% to 0.164 MtCO2e (Scope 1 −12%, Scope 2 market-based −28%, location-based −8%, Scope 3 excl. Cat. 15 −7%); total market-based footprint increased 11% to 26.94 MtCO2e, highlighting the dominance of financed emissions.
- Target setting and transition planning: Belfius prioritizes targets where it controls sources (own operations) and is developing science-based targets for financing and investment activities, starting with most material and climate-sensitive sectors; validation expected in 2025; a structured transition plan aligned with Strategy 2030 will follow; no significant Capex/Opex currently allocated.
- Disclosure scope and exclusions: publishes Scope 3 Cat. 15 only where methodologies exist; excludes insurance-associated emissions, assets under management (EUR 34.7bn), and local public sector entities (EUR 18bn) due to methodological gaps or uncertainty; monitoring methodological developments closely.
- Financed emissions methodology coverage: PCAF applied to seven asset classes plus financial lease (using real estate/energy/transport approaches), covering 63% of total loans and investments; remaining exposures mainly local public sector and financial corporations not yet covered due to lack of established methodology.

nodes.title: GHG Emissions - Introduction
nodes.heading: 2.2. GHG Emissions
nodes.start_phrase: Belfius yearly measures and discloses its GHG emissions across all its operations according to the GHG Protocol and PCAF methodologies.
nodes.summary: Overview of Belfius’ GHG emissions measurement and targets, using GHG Protocol and PCAF (incl. 2022 PCAF European building emissions factors for mortgages/CRE and 2021 PCAF factors for other asset classes). Belfius prioritizes targets for emissions it directly controls (own operations) and is developing science-based targets for financing and investment activities focused on the most material, climate‑sensitive sectors, with validation expected in 2025 and a transition plan aligned to Strategy 2030; currently no significant capex/opex is allocated. Key metrics (tCO2e): financed emissions (Scope 3 Cat.15, incl. sovereign) 22,456,424 (2022), 24,200,006 (2023), 26,780,024 (2024, +11% YoY); operational emissions 177,463 (2022), 176,835 (2023), 163,843 (2024, −7%), comprising Scope 1 1,873 (2024), Scope 2 market‑based 57 (2024) and Scope 3 (excl. Cat.15) 161,913 (2024); total market‑based footprint 22,633,887 (2022), 24,376,841 (2023), 26,943,867 (2024, +11%). Scope 3 Cat.15 is disclosed only where methodologies exist; emissions for insurance‑associated activities, assets under management (EUR 34.7bn at 31/12/2024) and local public sector entities (EUR 18bn at 31/12/2024) are not disclosed; insurance emissions are preliminarily deemed insignificant but uncertain.

nodes.title: Financed emissions
nodes.heading: 2.2.1. Financed emissions
nodes.start_phrase: Belfius calculates its financed emissions in accordance with the methodology of PCAF.
nodes.summary:
- The excerpt is from Belfius Bank’s 2024 Annual Report Sustainability Statement, focusing on climate targets, carbon accounting, and emissions performance.
- Belfius is developing science-based targets for financed and investment emissions, prioritizing the most material, climate-sensitive sectors and portfolio segments; validation is expected in 2025, with a structured transition plan aligned to Strategy 2030 to follow. No significant Capex/Opex is currently allocated to implementation.
- Overall carbon footprint (market-based) rose 11% from 24.38 MtCO2e in 2023 to 26.94 MtCO2e in 2024, driven by financed emissions.
- Financed emissions (Scope 3, Category 15, incl. sovereign) increased 11% to 26.78 MtCO2e in 2024.
- Operational emissions fell 7% to 163.8 ktCO2e in 2024: Scope 1 down 12% (1.9 kt), Scope 2 market-based down 28% (0.06 kt), and Scope 3 (excl. Cat. 15) down 7% (161.9 kt).
- Financed emissions are calculated per PCAF across seven asset classes (mortgages; business and corporate loans; commercial real estate; equity and bonds; motor vehicle loans; project finance; sovereign debt) and include financial leasing; these cover 63% of total loans and investments. Data quality scores are around 4.7–5.0.
- 2024 in-scope portfolio (excl. sovereign): €87.1bn carrying amount; 5.72 MtCO2e Scope 1&2 and 18.07 MtCO2e Scope 3; intensity 66 tCO2e/M€.
- Sovereign debt is reported separately to avoid double counting; Belfius applies the PCAF production-based approach (aligned with UNFCCC). 2024 sovereign emissions: 2.919 MtCO2e including LULUCF and 2.993 MtCO2e excluding LULUCF, on €10.5bn exposure.
- Certain categories are excluded due to lacking established methodologies: insurance-associated emissions, assets under management (AUM), and local public sector entities. Belfius will monitor methodology developments. Reference values: AUM €34.7bn and local public sector loans/investments €18bn (as of 31 Dec 2024). Insurance-associated emissions are preliminarily deemed insignificant but not disclosed due to uncertainty.
- The section transitions to “Operational emissions” (2.2.2), noting that material impacts and risks identified via the DMA will follow.

nodes.title: Operational emissions
nodes.heading: 2.2.2. Operational emissions
nodes.start_phrase: As a result of the DMA, the following Impacts and Risks have been identified as material:
nodes.summary:
- Financed emissions overview (2023–2024): Detailed PCAF-based inventory across asset classes (mortgages, business and corporate loans, commercial real estate, equity and bonds, financial lease, motor vehicle loans, project finance). Year-over-year shifts include:
  - Mortgages: scope 1&2 emissions down (1,297 to 1,211 kt CO2e) with stable data quality (5.00).
  - Business and corporate loans: scope 1&2 up (2,221 to 2,353 kt), scope 3 up (14,717 to 16,933 kt), intensity stable at 80 tCO2e/M€ (quality 4.38).
  - Commercial real estate: slight scope 1&2 increase (633 to 655 kt), intensity ~99 tCO2e/M€ (quality 5.00).
  - Equity and bonds: scope 1&2 down (1,165 to 1,064 kt), scope 3 up slightly (1,067 to 1,134 kt), intensity ~319 tCO2e/M€ (quality ~4.34).
  - Motor vehicle loans: scope 1&2 roughly flat (268 to 267 kt) with improving intensity (180 to 168 tCO2e/M€).
  - Project finance: near-zero reported emissions.
  - Totals: In-scope scope 1&2 slightly down (5,752 to 5,721 kt), scope 3 up (15,784 to 18,067 kt); overall intensity improves (68 to 66 tCO2e/M€); PCAF data quality score stable (~4.75).
- Sovereign debt emissions: Reported separately to avoid double counting. Methodology per PCAF with four options (production/consumption, with/without LULUCF). Belfius adopts production-based in line with UNFCCC. 2024 sovereign exposure increased (gross carrying amount 10,472 M€), production emissions 2,919 kt CO2e including LULUCF and 2,993 kt excluding LULUCF (up from 2023). Grand total including sovereign debt rises to 8,713 kt (scope 1&2) and 18,067 kt (scope 3); data quality score ~4.78.
- Operational climate IROs: Material impacts/risks identified include own GHG footprint, role in energy transition, and physical/operational risks if adaptation investments lag.
- Operational emissions results (excluding financed emissions): Full scope 1, 2, and 3 accounting with category detail and data-quality ratings.
  - Scope 1: Down 12% YoY to 1,873 tCO2e; heating lower, company car emissions lower, refrigerants up sharply.
  - Scope 2 (market-based): Down 29% to 56 tCO2e; location-based electricity shown separately.
  - Scope 3 operational (market-based): Down 7% to 161,914 tCO2e. Upstream dominated by capital goods; minor changes across commuting, business travel, waste. Downstream (excl. financed) down 14%, with leased assets the largest share.
  - Total operational footprint down ~8% YoY (market-based 163,844 tCO2e; location-based 167,218 tCO2e).
- Energy consumption and mix: Total energy use decreased (21,664 to 20,294 MWh). Renewables share increased from 61% to 65% via green electricity; fossil share declined; nuclear roughly stable at ~1%.
- GHG emissions intensity: 2024 intensity 8.3 kgCO2e per euro of net revenue (both market- and location-based), calculated including scope 3 category 15; net revenue €3.259bn.
- Targets and governance for own operations:
  - Targets approved by governance bodies; implementation overseen by the Own Operations Desk with technical oversight by a Climate Technical Decision Committee (ESG and risk/data leaders).
  - SBTi-aligned methodology using 1.5°C scenarios where available; 2022 baseline; primary horizon 2030 with future milestones toward 2050.
  - Covers buildings management, fleet and employee transport, and Belfius Auto Lease client activities.
  - Belfius not excluded from EU Paris-aligned Benchmarks eligibility based on revenue sources.
  - Quantification of decarbonisation levers to be finalized in 2025.

nodes.title: Operational emissions - Introduction
nodes.heading: 2.2.2. Operational emissions
nodes.start_phrase: As a result of the DMA, the following Impacts and Risks have been identified as material:
nodes.summary: This section outlines Belfius Bank’s material operational climate impacts and risks from its DMA, including contributing GHG emissions, participation in the energy transition, and the risk from not investing in adaptation infrastructure and technology, all within its own operations. It defines the operational footprint as scopes 1, 2 and 3 (excluding financed emissions) and provides 2022–2024 emissions by scope and category with 2024 data quality. In 2024, total operational footprint was 163,844 tCO2e market-based (-8% YoY; location-based 167,218), with Scope 1 at 1,873 tCO2e (-12%; heating 1,212, company cars 486, refrigerants up to 176), Scope 2 market-based at 56 tCO2e (-29%; location-based electricity 1,545, -8%), and Scope 3 operational at 161,914 tCO2e (-7%; upstream 97,631, downstream 64,301). Key 2024 Scope 3 categories include capital goods 86,712, employee commuting 3,504, business travel 630, downstream leased assets 55,169, franchises 8,362, waste 48; categories 9–10 are non-existent. Reported 2024 data quality: Scope 1 84%, Scope 2 13%, Scope 3 62%. Energy use in 2024 totaled 20,294 MWh with 65% renewable (all green electricity), 34% fossil, 1% nuclear. GHG emissions intensity was 8.3 kgCO2e/€ based on net revenue €3,259,288,443 and includes Scope 3 category 15.

nodes.title: Targets on operational emissions
nodes.heading: 2.2.2.1. Targets on operational emissions
nodes.start_phrase: Belfius climate targets are developed first on emissions for which Belfius fully controls.
nodes.summary:
- Presents Belfius Bank’s 2023–2024 operational energy mix and consumption: total energy use fell from 21,664 MWh to 20,294 MWh; renewables’ share rose from 61% to 65%; fossil energy declined (38% to 34%); nuclear steady at 1%; biofuels/biogas at 0; green electricity consumption reached 96.3% of total electricity in 2024.
- Discloses 2024 GHG emissions intensity at 8.3 kgCO2e per euro of net revenue (location- and market-based identical), with Scope 3 category 15 included; net revenue used: €3.259bn.
- Explains governance and methodology for operational emissions targets: Board/JMC approval; Own Operations Desk monitors; Climate Technical Decision Committee advises on methods; targets aligned to SBTi using primarily a 1.5°C pathway; 2022 set as the baseline year; main targets aim for 2030, with further milestones to come; indicates alignment with EU Paris-aligned Benchmark exclusions on fossil revenue.
- Details decarbonization targets:
  - Absolute reduction: −42% by 2030 across Scope 1 (buildings, company cars) and key Scope 3 categories (upstream energy, waste, business travel, employee commuting, franchises). 2022 baseline 23,583 tCO2e; 2024 at 14,924 tCO2e.
  - Intensity targets: leased car fleet −50% gCO2e/km by 2030 (driven by electrification/fuel switching, supported by Belgian incentives); leased real estate −64.7% kgCO2e/m² by 2030 (data and control depend on tenants).
  - Renewable electricity: 100% by 2025 for head/regional offices, salaried agencies, Crefius, Elantis; two buildings still on grey contracts in 2024.
- Notes 2024 progress drivers: accelerated electrification of the fleet and switching franchises to green electricity.
- Outlines three-pillar action plan for own operations:
  - Responsible building management (Scopes 1, 2, and 3 for leased/franchise assets): energy efficiency, renewable energy procurement/production, climate adaptation, waste reduction, responsible water management.
  - Green mobility (Scopes 1 & 3): employee fleet, commuting, business travel, and sustainable leasing offers.
  - Sustainable IT (Scope 3): lower tech footprint, extend device lifecycles, refurbish/donate, awareness campaigns (e.g., digital clean-up), and e-learning on climate.
- Lists concrete building actions: monitoring optimization; relocation to a more efficient Crefius building; nanogrids in salaried agencies; solar panels at Elantis; planned heat pump at Rogier Tower; EPC analyses; franchise emissions reduction offers (DVV); platform to automate tenant emissions data for leased assets.
- Describes climate adaptation and resilience: annual assessment of physical climate risks to critical assets (e.g., data center), redundancy and continuity measures to mitigate extreme events.
- Confirms ongoing waste management measures to prevent waste, increase recycling, and ensure responsible disposal.

nodes.title: Belfius’ targets
nodes.heading: 2.2.2.2. Belfius’ targets
nodes.start_phrase: Belfius aims to reduce its own emissions by setting emission reduction targets.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Belfius’ operational emissions-reduction targets and actions, use of carbon credits, and treatment of climate and environmental risks.
- Three-pillar plan to cut own emissions:
  - Responsible building management (scopes 1, 2, and scope 3 for buildings leased by Belfius Insurance): energy efficiency and renewable energy, climate adaptation, waste reduction, and water stewardship.
  - Green mobility (scopes 1 and 3): employee commuting, company fleet, and sustainable mobility offerings via Belfius Auto Lease.
  - Sustainable IT (scope 3): lower tech footprint, extend device lifecycles, refurbish/donate equipment, awareness and training, eco-design/coding.
- Buildings and energy:
  - Target 100% certified green electricity in all owned buildings and operations by end-2025; increase onsite renewables.
  - Most sites on green electricity; actions include energy monitoring optimization, moving to a more efficient building, nanogrids in branches, solar panels; planned heat pump at HQ, EPC analyses, better tenant data collection.
  - Climate adaptation via annual physical risk/threat analysis, multi-site critical activity execution, and resilient technologies.
- Waste and water:
  - Paperless policy and digitization; waste sorting and recycling across sites; new eco-friendly catering (vegetarian options), replacing paper cups with reusable cups by March 2025, targets for composting/biogas and eliminating single-use plastics.
  - 2024 waste roughly stable vs 2023; residual waste up, paper/cardboard down, recycled and biowaste up; e-waste excluded due to leasing.
  - Centralized water monitoring; nanogrids for local offices by 2025; telework has reduced water use since 2019.
- Green mobility (employees and leasing):
  - Telework and mobility incentives reduce commuting emissions; public transport fully reimbursed; active mobility allowances; parking fees discourage solo car use.
  - Fleet policy: since May 2023 only BEVs can be ordered; early 2025 fleet ~29% BEV, 34% hybrid; full fleet decarbonization by end-2029. Dynamic EV catalogue and options for shared/rental cars; plan to offer second-life leasing in 2026; 1,502 home chargers installed.
  - Federal mobility budget: ~50% of eligible employees opted in after one year; extended to Belfius Insurance in 2024.
  - Belfius Auto Lease: target -50% average CO2 per car-year by 2025 vs 2022 via electrification and MaaS; partnerships for charging (CenEnergy), mobility app/payment/budget platform (Skipr) with CO2 reporting; bike leasing via Cyclis.
  - Business travel: small share; 6% drop 2024 vs 2023 due to fewer long-haul flights.
- Sustainable IT:
  - Technology ~0.022% of total emissions; measurement complex and influenced by business choices and AI.
  - 2024 actions: ESG KPIs for tech leaders, laptop lifespan extended from 3 to 4 years, 1,500+ devices refurbished for schools, climate e-learning for staff; eco-design/coding handbook created, to be developed/tested in 2025.
- Carbon credits:
  - Voluntary purchase to cover emissions under highest direct control (excluding Auto Lease, financed emissions, DVV franchises); disclosed but not counted as footprint reductions.
  - Credits canceled: 44,600 tCO2e (2023) and 30,500 (2024); 100% reduction projects, 100% Gold Standard; no EU origin or corresponding adjustments.
  - Monitoring market integrity (e.g., ICVCM); all past credits canceled; future focus shifts from carbon credits to carbon removal credits.
- Climate and environmental risks:
  - C&E risks identified as top risks for Belfius, consistent with WEF assessments; long-term climate risk seen as most significant.
  - Belfius applies a holistic approach that integrates social impacts alongside financial effects of climate and environmental factors.

nodes.title: Climate and environmental risks
nodes.heading: 2.3. Climate and environmental risks
nodes.start_phrase: There is no doubt that climate change and environmental degradation (including biodiversity loss, pollution, and natural resources depletion) will have a significant and lasting impact on economic growth and prosperity.
nodes.summary:
- IT and employee engagement actions:

nodes.title: Climate and environmental risks - Introduction
nodes.heading: 2.3. Climate and environmental risks
nodes.start_phrase: There is no doubt that climate change and environmental degradation (including biodiversity loss, pollution, and natural resources depletion) will have a significant and lasting impact on economic growth and prosperity.
nodes.summary: Introductory overview of Belfius Bank’s approach to climate and environmental (C&E) risks, identifying them as top risks aligned with WEF 2023–2024 reports; defines physical risks (acute weather/natural disasters; chronic shifts like sea-level rise, water stress, biodiversity loss) and transition risks (policy, technological, market, legal, reputational), assessed separately over a 5-year strategic horizon and longer terms. Describes a flexible, phased-in climate risk assessment program to identify risk drivers across activities, portfolios, geographies; evaluate vulnerability of assets, portfolios and insurance coverages; flag material exposures; and, where possible, quantify impacts on profitability, solvency and liquidity, noting current data/methodology limitations preclude precise figures. nodes.title: Financial resilience analysis
nodes.heading: 2.3.1. Financial resilience analysis
nodes.start_phrase: The climate resilience assessments for financial risk cover the downstream value chain and differ per entity/activity.
nodes.summary:
- The document outlines Belfius’ climate and environmental (C&E) risk assessment framework aimed at identifying risk drivers, assessing portfolio and asset vulnerabilities, flagging material exposures, and quantifying potential financial impacts where possible.
- It adopts a phased, flexible approach due to immature methodologies and data gaps; precise financial impact figures are not yet provided.
- Both physical risks (acute events like storms, floods, fires; chronic changes like sea-level rise, water stress, biodiversity loss) and transition risks (policy, technology, market, legal, reputational) are defined and assessed separately.
- Time horizons include the 5-year strategic planning window and longer-term horizons, reflecting the expectation of rising C&E risks over time.
- Risk identification and assessment inform strategy and risk management, enabling monitoring and mitigation to ensure short-, medium-, and long-term resilience.
- Outputs are used to refine credit analysis in vulnerable sectors, prioritize data collection for higher transition-risk exposures, inform ESG strategy, enhance climate stress scenarios with deep dives, and identify mitigation measures and action plans.
- C&E risks affect Belfius mainly indirectly through financing activities, but also directly via own assets, insurance coverages, operations, business continuity, and reputation.
- The report distinguishes financial resilience (section 2.3.1) and group-wide operational resilience (section 2.3.2); financial resilience analyses cover the downstream value chain and differ by entity/activity (Belfius Bank vs. Belfius Insurance).
- Overall conclusion to date: while material, C&E risks do not currently pose a significant threat to profitability, solvency, or liquidity under the assessed scenarios; resilience is supported by a climate-aware strategy, robust risk framework, strong balance sheet, and reinsurance.
- Assessment approach: a two-step process—(1) high-level qualitative/quantitative materiality assessment; (2) deep dives and climate stress testing for material exposures to test resilience, capital adequacy, and adherence to risk appetite.
- Methodologies are aligned with UNEP FI, TCFD, supervisory guidance (ECB, EIOPA), and insights from NGFS, IEA, academia, and market best practices.
- For Belfius Bank, portfolio-level assessments by prudential risk category (credit, strategic/business, operational, market, liquidity) translate generic transmission channels (property damage, business disruption, income loss, higher costs/investments, lower profitability/asset values, inflation/productivity effects) into Belfius-specific financial impacts.
- Supplementary measures include portfolio climate stress tests on credit risk and counterparty-level ESG scoring via an in-house methodology.
- Forthcoming sections detail methodology and scenario use (2.3.1.1.1), results (2.3.1.1.2), disclosures on assets at material risk (2.3.1.1.3), and mitigation actions (2.3.1.1.4); the process flow runs from risk identification to materiality assessment to quantitative stress testing.

nodes.title: Financial resilience analysis - Introduction
nodes.heading: 2.3.1. Financial resilience analysis

Overall conclusion: while C&E risks are material, they currently do not pose a significant threat to profitability, solvency, or liquidity under the assessed scenarios. Belfius applies a two-step approach: an initial high-level materiality assessment using qualitative and quantitative data, followed—where risks are material—by deep-dive analyses and/or climate stress tests to evaluate financial impact, internal capital adequacy under severe but plausible scenarios, and adherence to risk appetite limits. Resilience is supported by a climate-aware strategy, robust balance sheet, and reinsurance program. Analyses draw on UNEP FI, TCFD, supervisory guidance (ECB, EOPIA), market best practices, academia, and organizations such as NGFS and IEA.

nodes.title: Financial Resilience analysis for Belfius Bank
nodes.heading: 2.3.1.1. Financial Resilience analysis for Belfius Bank
nodes.start_phrase: The financial resilience analysis describes the resilience of Belfius Bank’s strategy and business model in relation to climate change.
nodes.summary:
- Key conclusion: Climate and environmental (C&E) risks are considered material for Belfius but, under assessed scenarios, do not currently pose a significant threat to profitability, solvency, or liquidity.
- Strategic stance: Belfius expects to remain resilient and grow through a climate-aware strategy, robust risk management, strong balance sheet structure, and reinsurance program amid the transition to a low-carbon, climate-resilient economy.
- Assessment approach: Two-step process—(1) high-level, qualitative and quantitative materiality assessment to identify risk drivers and potential financial impacts; (2) deep dives and climate stress tests for material portfolios to quantify impacts, test resilience, and check alignment with risk appetite and internal capital adequacy.
- Standards and inputs: Uses UNEP FI, TCFD, supervisory guidance (ECB, EIOPA), best market practices, academic/scientific research, and insights from NGFS and IEA.
- Financial resilience analysis scope:
  - Portfolio-level assessments across prudential risk categories (credit, strategic/business, operational, market, liquidity) translating generic economic impacts (e.g., property damage, business disruption, income loss, higher costs/investments, lower profitability/asset values, inflation, productivity changes) into Belfius-specific financial impacts.
  - Climate stress tests focused on credit risk for selected portfolios.
  - Counterparty-level ESG assessment via an in-house ESG Score methodology.
  - Linked sections: methodology (2.3.1.1.1), results (2.3.1.1.2), disclosures on assets at material risk (2.3.1.1.3), and mitigation actions (2.3.1.1.4).
- Challenges and stance: Recognizes complexity of multi-channel C&E risk transmission and market data limitations; applies a flexible, phased approach and awaits further regulatory guidance.
- CERMA methodology (materiality assessment):
  - Conducted in 2023 with external climate and internal banking experts; covers short (to 2026), medium (2026–2030), and long term (2050); applied to the consolidated scope.
  - Reviewed at least biennially; not repeated in 2024 due to no material portfolio or hazard changes; scheduled for 2025.
  - Steps: qualitative identification of material risk drivers at portfolio level, followed by quantitative methods where relevant to find risk pockets and estimate potential financial impacts.
- Scenario design:
  - Transition risk: Belgian CORE-95 scenario (federal pathway to climate neutrality by 2050 with ~95% emissions reduction vs. 1990 and ~5% negative emissions), implying high transition risks.
  - Physical risk: RCP 8.5 “hot house” scenario (insufficient global mitigation, severe physical impacts including sea-level rise), used as a worst-case physical risk lens.
  - Additional targeted sensitivity analyses for specific risk dimensions.
- Forthcoming disclosures: Shares of assets exposed to material physical or transition risks and the bank’s mitigation measures are addressed in subsequent sections.

nodes.start_phrase: The financial resilience analysis describes the resilience of Belfius Bank’s strategy and business model in relation to climate change.
nodes.summary: Introduction to Belfius Bank’s climate and environmental (C&E) financial resilience analysis, outlining a three-part approach: (1) portfolio-level high‑level materiality assessments across prudential risk categories (credit, strategic and business, operational, market, liquidity) to identify sensitive portfolios and translate generic economic impacts into Belfius-specific financial impacts based on exposures, maturities, and risk profiles; (2) climate stress tests simulating the evolution of credit risk in selected portfolios under prominent C&E risk drivers; and (3) counterparty-level ESG assessments via an in-house methodology producing an ESG Score. Key risk drivers and transmission channels include property damage, business disruption, income loss, higher costs/investments, lower profitability/asset values, and macro effects such as price increases and labor productivity declines. The CERMA flow (risk identification → materiality assessment → stress testing) underpins the process. References: methodology (2.3.1.1.1), results (2.3.1.1.2), disclosures on the share of assets at material physical or transition risks (2.3.1.1.3), and mitigation actions (2.3.1.1.4). The bank notes data limitations, cross-risk complexities, and a flexible, gradual approach pending further regulatory guidance.

nodes.title: Scope and methodology of assessments
nodes.heading: 2.3.1.1.1 Scope and methodology of assessments
nodes.start_phrase: The potential impact of C&E risks on Belfius Bank’s risk profile was assessed in 2023 with the support of external climate experts and internal banking experts.
nodes.summary:
- Belfius Bank highlights that climate and environmental (C&E) risks affect multiple financial risk categories via diverse drivers and transmission channels, making assessment challenging amid limited market data; the bank adopts a flexible, gradual approach and anticipates further regulatory guidance.
- Scope and methodology center on the Climate and Environmental Risks Materiality Assessment (CERMA), performed in 2023 with external climate and internal banking experts to gauge impacts across micro/macro channels and time horizons: short (to 2026), medium (2026–2030), and long term (2050). The assessment covers the consolidated bank, is reviewed at least biennially, was not repeated in 2024 due to no material changes, and is planned for 2025.
- CERMA process: initial qualitative portfolio-level materiality screening (considering time horizons, risk drivers, risk dimensions, and vulnerability clusters), followed by quantitative analyses where feasible to identify risk pockets and estimate high-level financial impacts.
- Scenario framework:
  - Belgian CORE-95 transition scenario: aligned with Belgium’s path to climate neutrality by 2050 (≈95% emissions reduction vs. 1990 plus ≈5% negative emissions), implying high transition risks due to the ambition level.
  - RCP 8.5 “hot house world” scenario: assumes insufficient global policy action, leading to severe physical risks and irreversible impacts; used as a worst-case for physical risk assessment.
- Additional targeted scenarios and sensitivity analyses are applied to the most material risk drivers and specific risk dimensions. Detailed assessments per risk category follow in subsequent chapters; non-financial risk is addressed separately in the non-financial resilience analysis (section 2.3.2).

nodes.title: Climate and environmental risks materiality assessment (CERMA)
nodes.heading: a. Climate and environmental risks materiality assessment (CERMA)
nodes.start_phrase: The potential impact of C&E risks on Belfius Bank’s risk profile was assessed in 2023 with the support of external climate experts and internal banking experts.
nodes.summary:
- Context and approach: Belfius Bank outlines the challenges of assessing climate and environmental (C&E) risks given data gaps and multi-channel transmission across financial risks. It adopts a flexible, gradual approach and expects further regulatory guidance.
- Scope and methodology (CERMA): A bank-wide Climate and Environmental Risks Materiality Assessment was performed in 2023 with internal and external experts, covering short (to 2026), medium (2026–2030), and long-term (to 2050) horizons. It will be reviewed at least biennially; not repeated in 2024 due to no material changes and scheduled for 2025. The process combines a qualitative portfolio-level materiality screen (by time horizon, risk drivers, risk dimensions, vulnerability clusters) followed by quantitative analysis where relevant.
- Core scenarios used:
  - Belgian CORE-95 transition scenario: ambitious pathway to climate neutrality by 2050 (95% emissions reduction vs. 1990 plus 5% negative emissions), implying high transition risks.
  - RCP 8.5 “hot house” scenario: insufficient global policy action leading to severe physical risks and irreversible impacts; used as a worst-case for physical risk.
  - Additional targeted sensitivity scenarios were applied to specific risk dimensions.
- Risk categories and assessment types:
  - Credit risk (enterprises & entrepreneurs): exposure-based and scenario-driven sensitivity analyses on loans and investment portfolios.
  - Credit risk (individuals): scenario-driven sensitivity on the mortgage portfolio.
  - Market risk: scenario-driven sensitivity on the trading book.
  - Liquidity risk: scenario-driven sensitivity on liquidity, buffers, and funding access/costs.
  - Strategic and business risk: expert-based risk cartography (competitive position, strategy, partnerships, governance).
  - Non-financial risk: expert-based risk cartography (own assets, operations, third parties); details in section 2.3.2.
- Credit risk detail:
  - Non-retail portfolios: sector-level, bottom-up analysis in Belgium-focused geographies, combining exposure analysis with sensitivity tests on sample counterparties and dynamic extrapolation across short, medium, and long terms.
  - Mortgage portfolio: scenario analysis of transition (renovation mandates/regulation) and physical (flood) risks. Stresses applied to:
    - PD via required renovation investments relative to borrower capacity.
    - LGD via collateral value haircuts for poor energy performance and flood exposure.
- Strategic and business risk detail: Qualitative assessment of vulnerabilities in competitive positioning, strategy design/implementation, partnerships, and governance; evaluates potential loss of customers, market share, and revenues due to external shifts and Belfius’ actions/commitments.
- Market risk detail: Recognition that C&E risks can trigger valuation shocks, higher volatility, and correlation breakdowns. Scenarios include:
  1) rising carbon prices; 2) Belgium–EU inflation differentials from uneven transition progress; 3) physical events affecting FX; 4) impacts on equity price/dividend volatility; 5) effects on corporate and sovereign bond values via credit and correlation trading spreads.
- Liquidity risk detail: Scenario-driven analysis of potential net cash outflows and buffer depletion transmitted through deposits, loans, credit/liquidity line drawdowns, and funding access/costs. Scenarios cover: 1) renovation costs affecting deposits/loans/credit lines; 2) C&E-related reputational impacts on loan production and deposits; 3) financing repairs after adverse physical events; 4) tighter collateral eligibility and higher haircuts reducing market funding and liquidity buffers.
- Climate stress testing for credit risk: Development of simulation tools and standalone climate stress tests, including a cashflow simulation model to quantify transition risk impacts on non-retail customers and investees.

nodes.title: Climate stress test for credit risk
nodes.heading: b. Climate stress test for credit risk
nodes.start_phrase: In order to better grasp the transmission channels of climate risks and quantify their potential impacts on the evolution of the risk profile of its loan and investment portfolios,
nodes.summary: This section of Belfius Bank’s 2024 Sustainability Statement outlines how climate and environmental (C&E) risks are assessed across key risk types and portfolios. It begins by noting potential losses of customers, market share, and revenues from shifts in the business environment and from inadequate climate actions. For market risk, it describes channels through which C&E risks can trigger asset price shocks, higher volatility, and correlation breakdowns, and defines five scenario analyses covering carbon price shocks, BE/EU inflation differentials, FX impacts from physical events, equity volatility via dividends/prices, and spread impacts on corporate/sovereign bonds (including correlation trading). For liquidity risk, it explains how C&E drivers could cause net cash outflows and strain liquidity buffers and tests four scenarios: renovation costs affecting deposits/loans/credit lines, C&E-related reputational effects on business volumes, funding reconstruction after physical events, and tighter collateral eligibility with higher haircuts. It details climate stress testing for credit risk: a cash-flow simulation tool for non-retail portfolios assessing transition risks over short, medium, and long horizons, focused on transition-sensitive sectors (Manufacturing, Energy, Construction, Commercial Real Estate) and UK Water & Gas bonds, under NGFS-derived Current Policies (low transition risk) and Net Zero (high transition risk) scenarios; and a mortgage tool projecting asset values and borrower creditworthiness under transition (EPC ratings, energy prices, renovation pace) and physical (Belgian flood maps with value haircuts) risks, aligned with NGFS pathways and emphasizing impacts to 2030 across Realistic Base Case, Net Zero, and Delayed Transition scenarios. Finally, it introduces an ESG Score for non-retail clients with turnover above €10 million to gauge sustainability performance and Belfius’s exposure to ESG risk drivers, independent of credit ratings and aggregating seven metrics into a single score.

nodes.title: ESG score
nodes.heading: C. ESG score
nodes.start_phrase: To objectively assess the ESG profile of non -retail clients, Belfius Bank has also developed an ESG Score, for corporates with more than 10 million turnover.
nodes.summary:
- The report outlines Belfius Bank’s climate risk assessment for (mid)corporates using a cash flow simulation tool that projects impacts from transition factors (e.g., higher CO2 and energy costs, green capex) across three horizons: short term (to 2026), medium term (2026–2030), and long term (2050).
- Initial analysis targets the most transition‑sensitive sectors based on exposure and CERMA results: Manufacturing, Energy, Construction, and Commercial Real Estate, plus UK Water & Gas for long‑dated run‑off bond portfolios. About 10 representative companies per sector were individually assessed.
- Two NGFS‑derived transition scenarios are applied: Current Policies (lower transition risk, policy status quo) and Net Zero (higher transition risk, ambitious policies to achieve carbon neutrality).

- For mortgage portfolios, a dedicated tool assesses:
  - Transition risks via EPC ratings, energy prices, and renovation pace under three scenarios aligned to NGFS pathways: Realistic Base Case (early, gradually stricter policies), Net Zero (rapid market shift over next five years), and Delayed Transition (policy delay, limited change to 2030).
  - Physical risks via flood exposure in Belgium, geolocating collateral to regional flood maps and applying value haircuts for medium–high risk zones. Simulations emphasize short–medium term impacts to 2030.

- Belfius developed an ESG Score for non‑retail corporates (>€10m turnover), independent of credit ratings, to assess client ESG performance and related bank risk exposure. It aggregates seven dimensions: client consciousness, exposure to ESG risks, ESG maturity, risk mitigation, overall performance, benchmark position, and forward‑looking plans.
  - Inputs are gathered through a client questionnaire, fostering dialogue on practices, challenges, and support needs.
  - Key Risk Indicators (KRIs), aligned with EBA practices, combine quantitative (e.g., CO2 emissions, energy use) and qualitative measures (e.g., policies, transition plans, targets, trends), with expert‑set weights and sector‑specific benchmarks. The model will be iteratively improved.
  - By 31/12/2024, approximately 400 companies/groups were scored; similar internal frameworks exist for Financial Institutions and Sovereigns.

- Risk identification and assessment conclude that climate and environmental (C&E) risks are material, but potential financial impacts for Belfius are manageable even long term, considering current and planned mitigations.
  - From an initial set of 46 risk drivers (33 physical, 13 transition) based on EU Taxonomy, UNEP FI, and TCFD, Belfius prioritized 17 physical and 13 transition risk drivers for deeper analysis, focused mainly on Belgium. The selection and methodologies will be refined as data and best practices evolve.
  - The section transitions into a detailed discussion of physical risks (A1 Physical risks).

nodes.title: Results of risk identification and assessment
nodes.heading: 2.3.1.1.2 . Results of risk identification and assessment
nodes.start_phrase: The overall outcome of the assessments shows that although C&E risks are deemed material, the potential financial impacts stemming from those risks for Belfius Bank remain fully manageable,
nodes.summary:
- Describes Belfius Bank’s internal ESG risk assessment framework for corporate clients, built around seven KRI dimensions: client ESG awareness, exposure to ESG risks, ESG maturity, ESG risk mitigation capacity, overall ESG performance (past and present), benchmark position versus peers, and forward-looking plans and commitments.
- Explains that data are collected via a client questionnaire embedded in a dialogue to surface practices, challenges, and (financial) support needs.
- Notes KRIs are selected and weighted by expert judgment, aligned with EBA parameters, and include quantitative metrics (e.g., CO2 emissions, energy use), qualitative factors (policies, transition plans, targets), and trend analyses; some KRIs are general vs. sector-specific to enable appropriate benchmarking.
- Emphasizes the model is iterative, with KRIs and weights subject to adjustment as it is evaluated and improved.
- Reports that by 31/12/2024, ESG risk profiles for about 400 companies/groups were completed, with analogous internal scoring frameworks developed for Financial Institutions and Sovereigns.
- Summarizes risk identification results: climate and environmental risks are material but the potential financial impacts for Belfius are considered fully manageable long term given existing and planned mitigating actions.
- Details the methodology to identify relevant C&E risks: from 46 initial risk drivers (33 physical, 13 transition) sourced from EU Taxonomy, UNEP FI, and TCFD, Belfius selected 13 key transition and 17 key physical risk drivers for its mainly Belgian portfolios, based on likelihood and impact severity, and conducted in-depth analyses of transmission channels and impacts.
- Indicates that ongoing improvements in data and methodologies may change the set of material risk drivers and sensitive portfolios/sectors going forward.

Results of risk identification and assessment   
The overall outcome of the assessments shows that although C&E risks are deemed material, the potential 
financial impacts stemming from those risks for Belfius Bank remain fully manageable, even in the long term, 
especially taking into consideration existing and future mitigating actions.

nodes.title: Identification of relevant C&E risks
nodes.heading: a. Identification of relevant C&E risks
nodes.start_phrase: Starting from a long list of 46 risk drivers (of which 33 for physical risk and 13 for transition risk), based on EU Taxonomy, UNEP FI and TCFD sources,
nodes.summary:
- Outlines Belfius Bank’s internal ESG client scoring framework, structured around seven dimensions: client ESG awareness, exposure to ESG risks, maturity of transition, risk mitigation capacity, overall ESG performance, peer benchmarking, and future-oriented plans.
- Describes data collection via a client-completed questionnaire, embedding a dialogue to surface practices, challenges, and financing needs.
- Details Key Risk Indicators (KRIs) aligned with EBA practices, each with expert-assigned weights; includes general vs sector-specific KRIs for benchmarking, and both quantitative (e.g., CO2, energy use) and qualitative metrics (policies, transition plans, targets), plus trend analyses. Notes ongoing model evaluation with potential KRI/weight adjustments.
- Reports coverage: by 31/12/2024, ESG profiles of about 400 companies/groups assessed; similar internal scoring methodologies exist for Financial Institutions and Sovereigns.
- Summarizes risk identification and assessment: climate and environmental (C&E) risks are material but potential financial impacts are assessed as fully manageable, even long term, considering mitigation measures.
- Explains the selection process of material risk drivers: from 46 initial drivers (33 physical, 13 transition) based on EU Taxonomy, UNEP FI, and TCFD, to 17 key physical and 13 key transition drivers for Belfius’s core geography (mainly Belgium), using likelihood and impact severity.
- Provides likelihood scales:
  - Physical risks: a 1–5 scale with definitions for acute (CDP-based), future likelihood (IPCC-based), and chronic hazards (expert assessment), indicating when critical thresholds may be permanently exceeded.
  - Transition risks: a 1–5 scale tied to policy/regulation status and sectoral sensitivity to market/technology/reputation shifts.
- Notes three time horizons (short to 2026, medium 2026–2030, long to 2050) and an expectation of increasing C&E risks over longer horizons, especially physical risks; emphasizes dependency on transition policies and adaptation measures and the need for regular updates as data and methodologies improve.
- Indicates CERMA results are presented as a relative ranking; credit risk is most material among prudential risks but remains manageable; further details will be provided in subsequent sections, with non-financial risk addressed under operational resilience.

nodes.title: Assessment of the impact of selected C&E risks
nodes.heading: b. Assessment of the impact of selected C&E risks
nodes.start_phrase: The results of the CERMA are presented in the table below.
nodes.summary:
- Part of Belfius Bank’s 2024 Annual Report (Management Report – Sustainability Statement) outlining climate and environmental (C&E) risk assessment and management.
- Defines a five-level sector sensitivity and likelihood scale (Very Low to Very High) linked to policy/regulation and market/technology/reputation drivers, with corresponding organizational response status (from “Not in discussion” to “Already in place and about to be strengthened”).
- Considers three time horizons (short to 2026, medium 2026–2030, long to 2050) and notes rising C&E risks over longer horizons, especially physical risks; underscores dependence on the pace and scale of transition policies and adaptation; commits to regularly revising drivers and transmission channels.
- Presents results of the Climate & Environmental Risk Materiality Assessment (CERMA) as a relative ranking; even the most material impacts are viewed as manageable since current/future mitigations are not yet factored in.
- Materiality by risk type:
  - Credit Risk: Significant. Transition policies, carbon pricing, and technology shifts could pressure revenues and costs in climate-sensitive sectors, triggering rating downgrades, higher cost of risk and RWAs; impact monitored via CET1 ratio.
  - Strategic & Business Risk: Moderate. Falling behind peers on sustainable products/strategy or negative market perceptions could lead to customer loss, profitability impacts, and a riskier client mix.
  - Non-Financial Risk: Moderate. Physical risks may disrupt Belfius and third parties; execution risks peak mid-term; long-term product/service substitution expected; legal and reputational risks may affect investors and talent.
  - Market Risk: Limited. Small exposures, short liquidity horizons, and hedging reduce potential asset devaluations and P&L impacts.
  - Liquidity Risk: Limited. Possible deposit outflows and liquidity buffer use would likely be gradual and manageable.
- Overall expectation that financial impacts remain limited, even long term, with gradual manifestation allowing proactive management to preserve a sound balance sheet and earnings capacity.
- Mitigation and strategy: ongoing and planned actions to support the Belgian transition, manage portfolio composition to reduce C&E exposure, and engage counterparties on transition pathways and physical risk adaptation; prioritization of higher-risk sectors for deeper analysis; further details referenced in the mitigation actions section.
- Next section signposts: climate resilience analysis on credit risk for non-retail portfolios, with sector-by-sector exposure review and risk driver importance (graph referenced).
